items.title: Review and Approval: Authorization Checks
items.author: Balazs_Szauder
items.text:
Challenge with Authorization Checks 
 The object being processed is the purchase order item; however, reviewers and/or approvers are generally not purchasers and will not have authorization to display the purchase order itself 
 Different types of users perform review/approval (Purchase Order Owner, Controller, or G/L Accountant), each requiring specific authorization checks fitting their role 
 Implementation of Authorization Checks 
 Role-specific authorization checks are implemented in the review and approval transactions 
 Authorization checks are implemented as the default implementation of BAdI BADI_FACRA_AUTH_CHECK in ABAP class CL_BADI_FACRA_AUTH_CHECK 
 The default implementation can be replaced by a customer-defined implementation 
 Authorization Checks by User Role 
 For Purchase Order Owners: 
 In review transaction FACRARVWBU, the purchase order owner is only allowed to review purchase order items where their UserID is entered as: 
 Goods recipient, OR 
 Requisitioner, OR 
 Creator 
 If defined as a substitute for another user in the workflow, they are also allowed to review the corresponding purchase order items of that user 
 Substitutes are defined in transaction SBWP menu: Settings → Workflow Settings → Edit Substitute (any substitution profile can be used) 
 Note: Workflow transaction SBWP is used for defining substitutes despite the workflow itself not being used for review by transactions FACRARVW* 
 For Controllers: 
 The Controller must have CO reporting authorization for the cost object for which they started review transaction FACRARVWCO 
 For G/L Accountants: 
 The G/L Accountant must have display authorization for the company code and/or business area for which they started approval transaction FACRAAPPRVGL 

 Users processing data with the Accrual Engine must possess specific authorizations for three authorization objects (viewable in transaction SU21): 
 F_ACES_DST – Accrual Engine in S4: Accrual Objects 
 F_ACES_PST – Accrual Engine in S4: Accrual Postings 
 F_ACES_PER – Accrual Engine in S4: Periodic Accrual Amounts 
 Additional Requirements for Reviewers and Approvers: 
 Reviewers and approvers must have these Accrual Engine-specific authorizations in addition to their user-role specific authorizations. 
 Authorization Checking Mechanism: 
 In review and approval transactions, authorizations for the F_ACES_PER authorization object are verified directly at the database level through the corresponding CDS view (DDL source), rather than at the ABAP runtime level. 
 Critical Troubleshooting Information: 
 If review/approval transactions fail to display records for a company code, the root cause is likely missing authorization for the F_ACES_PER authorization object. This missing authorization cannot be detected through transaction SU53 because the check occurs at the database level rather than during ABAP runtime execution.

items.title: Review and Approval: Process Steps
items.author: Balazs_Szauder
items.text:
The following four steps comprise the review and/or approval process for periodic accruals: 
 1. Generate Proposals 
 Proposal accrual amounts must be generated before review or approval can be performed at the end of the fiscal period 
 Generated using transaction ACEPROPOSALRUN, which: 
 Calculates and saves planned costs 
 Calculates and saves actual costs (by summarizing posted supplier invoices, etc.) 
 Calculates accruals (as planned costs minus actual costs) 
 Typically executed after the last invoice and goods receipt are posted for the fiscal period, but can also be executed mid-period 
 When executed mid-period, actual costs and accruals may not be final; however, planned costs can be correctly calculated by the accrual method, allowing review of planned costs/PoC to begin 
 2. Perform Review of Proposed Amounts Role-specific transactions are available for reviewing accruals or planned costs/PoC: 
 Purchase Order Owner : Transaction FACRARVWBU (Note: Only review is supported in release 1809; approval is not yet supported) 
 Controller : Transaction FACRARVWCO (Note: Only review is supported in release 1809; approval is not yet supported) 
 3. Perform Approval of Proposed or Reviewed Accrual Amounts 
 Approval can be performed in addition to or instead of review 
 Only the G/L Accountant is currently supported as approver: 
 G/L Accountant : Transaction FACRAAPPRVGL (Note: Only approval is supported in release 1809; review is not yet supported) 
 4. Post the Accruals 
 After review/approval is completed, accruals can be posted using transaction ACEPOSTINGRUN

items.title: Review and Approval: Supported User Roles
items.author: Balazs_Szauder
items.text:
The Accrual Engine proposes periodic accrual amounts that require review and/or approval from designated user roles: 
 Purchase Order Owner 
 This role involves someone with detailed knowledge of the purchase order, typically a project lead or cost center responsible party 
 Considered the preferred person to evaluate the progress and accruals of the purchase order 
 The system supports multiple methods to identify the purchase order owner: the goods recipient of the PO item, the PO requestor (requisitioner), or the creator of the PO 
 Controller 
 Involved in the review/approval process because accrual posting means posting of costs, which affects the budget of cost centers 
 Serves as a fallback option if the purchase order owner cannot be reached in time to perform the required review/approval 
 G/L Accountant 
 Interested in accrual amounts because they impact the gain/loss reported in the P&L statement 
 Concerned with year-end implications, as accrual amounts affect the taxes the company must pay on its gain

items.title: Optional Period End Closing Activity: Review and Approve Accrual Amounts
items.author: Balazs_Szauder
items.text:
Default Calculation Method: The Accrual Engine calculates periodic accrual amounts using the formula: planned costs minus actual costs. This calculation method assumes that planned costs accurately reflect reality. 
 Concrete Example: 
 Date: 31.05.2018 
 Purchase Order: 4711, Item 10 
 Proposed Accrual Amount: 2,000 EUR 
 Planned Costs: 5,000 EUR 
 Posted Invoices (Actual Costs): 3,000 EUR 
 Calculation: 5,000 EUR - 3,000 EUR = 2,000 EUR accrual 
 Basis of Planned Costs: The 5,000 EUR in planned costs was derived by linearizing the PO item net value of 12,000 EUR across the purchase order's lifetime—spanning from the PO creation date (01/2012) to the planned final delivery date (12/2018). 
 Underlying Assumption: The 2,000 EUR accrual amount assumes that the company has already received goods or services valued at 5,000 EUR, but the corresponding invoice has not yet been posted (e.g., because the supplier has not sent it). 
 Nature of Accrual Proposals: The accrual amounts calculated by the Accrual Engine are merely proposals based on assumptions, not definitive figures. 
 Review Necessity: Given the assumption-based nature of these calculations, it is essential that a qualified person reviews and/or approves the proposed accruals to validate whether the underlying assumption is correct. 
 Best Practice Recommendation: Rather than reviewing accrual amounts directly, it is recommended to review the planned costs instead. 

 Review of Planned Costs Instead of Accruals 
 Default Configuration: 
 The Accrual Engine calculates accruals as planned costs minus actual costs (default and recommended setting) 
 When using this method, the review process should be activated for planned costs rather than accrual amounts 
 Rationale for Reviewing Planned Costs: 
 Reviewer Expertise : Reviewers are often project leads or other non-accounting personnel who lack understanding of accrual accounting concepts 
 Late Invoice/Goods Receipt Handling : Accruals automatically reduce when invoices or goods receipts arrive after the review/approval phase is complete 
 Progress Representation : 
 Planned costs represent actual project progress 
 Accruals represent only the missing/outstanding costs 
 When percentage of completion is reviewed, planned costs (not accruals) accurately reflect this progress metric 
 Key Point: Although reviewing planned costs may seem counterintuitive initially, it is more practical and suitable than directly reviewing accrual amounts for the reasons outlined above. 

 Difference between Review And Approval 
 The Accrual Engine implements review and approval of periodic accrual amounts with the following characteristics: 
 Review Process: 
 Review is always optional 
 If no one reviews the proposed accrual amounts for a purchase order item, the system automatically posts the proposed amount 
 Approval Process: 
 Approval is mandatory for posting 
 The system only posts the proposed accrual amount for a purchase order item if the approver grants approval 
 Concurrent Implementation: 
 Both review and approval steps can be active simultaneously 
 This enables a 4-eye principle (dual control) system where, for example, the purchase order owner performs the review and a G/L accountant performs the approval 
 Adjustment Capabilities: 
 Both reviewers and approvers can adjust the proposed accrual amounts or planned costs 
 When adjusting amounts, users must enter a reason code and may optionally add a comment explaining the adjustment 
 The system creates change documents each time a user adjusts an amount 
 Change documents can be displayed using transaction POACTREE03 (Display Changes) 
 Attachments can be added in review and approval screens to provide further explanation for any accrual amount or planned cost adjustments 

 Review and Approval by Purchase Order Owner 
 Role and Purpose: 
 The purchase order owner is designated as the most qualified person to evaluate the purchase order's progress (measured by percentage of completion) and associated accruals. 
 Potential Purchase Order Owner Categories: 
 Three different user types can serve as the purchase order owner: 
 Requisitioner of the Purchase Order Item 
 The user who requested the creation of the purchase order 
 Goods Recipient of the Purchase Order Item 
 The user who will receive the ordered goods or services 
 Creator of the Purchase Order 
 The person who created the purchase order in the system 
 Reference: 
 The selection screen of the review transaction FACRARVWBU provides additional details on these purchase order owner designations. 

 Review Screen: Transaction FACRARVWCO 

 Review And Approval Screen: Additional Fields 

 Review And Approval Screen: Additional Fields: Exampl es 

 Display Reviewed Accruals in Transaction POACTREE03 
 Purpose: 
 Transaction POACTREE03 is used to display accrual objects and provides the ability to verify review-related information for accruals. 
 Information Available: 
 The transaction allows users to check: 
 Which user performed the review 
 Which amounts the reviewer adjusted 
 The periods in which adjustments were made 
 Conditional Availability: 
 If review is activated for planned costs, the review information becomes available specifically for the item type that represents the planned costs (as shown in the accompanying screenshot). 

 Reviewers are Sometimes not Accountants 
 Reviewer Profile: 
 Review of periodic accrual amounts must be performed by users with detailed knowledge of the corresponding purchase order—specifically the purchase order owner. These reviewers can include: 
 Project leads in consulting projects 
 Cost center responsibles acting as goods recipients of the purchase order item 
 Post-Review Invoice Problem: 
 After review completion, additional invoices may be posted, which must correspondingly reduce the accruals. 
 Resolution: Total Costs Approach: 
 The issue is resolved by having reviewers revise the "total" costs expected at period-end, rather than revising the accrual amount directly. 
 Mechanism: 
 Total costs comprise: 
 Actual costs (e.g., invoices) + Accruals 
 When an additional invoice is posted: 
 Actuals increase by the invoice amount 
 Accruals automatically decrease by the same amount 
 Total costs remain unchanged 
 The revised total costs represent the reviewed and optionally adjusted planned costs for the period. 

 Review: Late Invoice Example 
 KBA 3806561 
 Review of Percentage of Completion 
 KBA 3806544 
 Review and Approval Transactions: Simplify Selection Screen 
 KBA 3806563

items.title: Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation and Review
items.author: Ujhelyi_Zsuzsi
items.text:
Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation: Available as of Release 1809 SP4 and 1909 SP1 
 Availability: 
 Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation is available starting from SAP S/4HANA Release 1809 SP4 (Support Package 4) and Release 1909 SP1 (Support Package 1) onwards. 
 For Earlier Versions: 
 If you are using an earlier support package than those specified above, you must apply SAP Note 2838538 titled "Accrual Engine: Quantity Based Calculation" to enable this functionality. 

 Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation: Motivation 
 Current Default Approach - Amount-Based: 
 By default, periodic accrual amounts are calculated using an amount-based approach. 
 Amount-based calculation ignores quantities in both planned costs and actual costs. 
 Accruals are calculated by simply subtracting actual costs from planned costs. 
 Limitations of Amount-Based Approach: 
 This approach ignores differences in both price and quantity between planned and actual costs. 
 When actual costs are posted with a different price, or with both a different price and different quantity compared to planned costs, calculating accruals based on amounts alone is inaccurate. 
 Example: When posting the supplier invoice a different price is used compared to the purchase order. 
 Advantages of Quantity-Based Approach: 
 Accuracy: 
 It is more accurate to calculate accruals by considering both planned and actual quantities alongside amounts. 
 Usability for Reviewers: 
 Quantity-based accruals are more useful for review purposes at the end of a fiscal period. 
 Amount-based reviews can be difficult for reviewers to validate as correct. 
 For non-accountant reviewers (such as project managers), reviewing quantities is more intuitive and natural than reviewing amounts. 
 Example: Purchasing of consulting. It is easier for the project manager to judge the number of man days compared to consulting costs. 
 Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation: Algorithm 
 Definition:  Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation means accrual amounts are calculated using the formula: 
 Accrual Amount = (Cumulated Planned Quantity − Cumulated Actual Quantity) × Net Price 
 How the Formula Works: 
 First, the accrual quantity is calculated as planned quantity minus actual quantity. 
 Afterwards, the accrual quantity is multiplied by the net price to get the accrual amount. 
 Net Price Source:  The Net Price in this formula is taken from the purchase order item. 
 Remark – Cases Where Quantity Is Not Considered: 
 In the below service PO Items, if the unit is unconvertible (namely, no dimension is defined for this unit), the quantity will not be considered: 
 Lean Service:  Product Type Group is 2 and Item Category is empty 
 Enhanced Limit:  Product Type Group is 2 and Item Category is E 
 Item Category is D 
 Some common unconvertible units are EA, PC, AU, etc., but whether they are convertible or not is defined in table  T006 Units of Measurement . 
 Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation: Customizing 
 Activation:  To activate the quantity-based calculation for accrual amounts, the indicator  Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation  must be set in the IMG activity: 
 Accruals Management → Basic Settings → Accrual Item Types → Define Accrual Item Types, in the section Item Type Settings for Ldrgrp incl. Repr. Ledger (see transaction  ACEIMG ). 
 Technically, this is customizing viewcluster  VC_TACE_ITEMTY . 
 Plan Minus Actual Approach:  If the Plan Minus Actual approach is used to calculate the accruals, the indicator Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation must be set  only for the accrual item type that calculates the accrual amounts . 
 In the default customizing settings, this is the accrual item type  ACCRL . 
 Do  not  set the indicator in the other two accrual item types for planned costs and actual costs. 
 Purpose of the Indicator:  The indicator only needs to be set for the accruals item type ( ACCRL ) so that the system uses the formula:  Accrual Amount = (Planned Quantity − Actual Quantity) × Net Price 
 In the planned costs and actual costs, the Accrual Engine anyway always has the quantities available. 
 By setting the indicator Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation for ACCRL, the Accrual Engine "just" switches: 
 From:  the standard formula:  Accrual Amount = Cumulated Planned Costs − Cumulated Actual Costs 
 To : the quantity-based formula:  Accrual Amount = (Cumulated Planned Quantity − Cumulated Actual Quantity) × Net Price 

 Amount-Based Accrual Calculation: Display of Quantities is Possible 
 Displaying quantities in the Accrual Engine screens is possible even if the accrual calculation is done amount-based. 
 In the amount-based approach—which is the default—the quantities are ignored when it comes to calculating the accrual amounts. 
 In transaction PACOTREE03, activating quantity-based accrual calculation affects "only" the algorithm of how the columns for the accrual amounts are calculated. 

 Quantity-Based Accrual Calculation: Example - Purchase Order 
 The effects of quantity-based accrual calculation are explained through an example. The example includes the following key points: 
 Starting point:  The example begins with the creation of a purchase order that has a delivery schedule with partial deliveries. 
 Goods receipt:  No goods receipt is expected. 
 Cost posting:  The costs will be posted by the supplier invoice.

items.title: Review and Approval process- Customizing
items.author: Ujhelyi_Zsuzsi
items.text:
Activation of Review and/or Approval Process 
 The review and/or approval process for periodic accrual amounts is activated through customizing settings in the Accrual Engine at three levels: company code, accrual item type, and ledger group. 
 Currency Limitations in Release 1809:  In release 1809, review activation is restricted to currency type 00 only, which allows reviewers and approvers to adjust proposed accrual amounts in transaction currency. All other currencies are set to read-only mode during the review process. 
 Configuration Location:  The configuration is performed in transaction ACEIMG through the IMG activity "Define Accrual Item Types → Item Type Settings for Ledgergroup and Representative Ledger." 
 Activation Options: 
 The "Review Active" checkbox activates the review process 
 The "Approval Required" checkbox activates the approval process 
 Applicable Accrual Item Types:  Review and/or approval processes can be activated exclusively for the planned costs accrual item type. These processes cannot be activated for the other two accrual item types: actual costs and accruals 

 Enable Multiple Currencies in Review & Approval Screens 
 Transaction Currency Limitation: 
 Adjusting periodic accrual amounts during review and/or approval is restricted to transaction currency only. 
 Additional Currency Display: 
 Additional currencies can be enabled as read-only fields in the review and approval screens. 
 Configuration Method: 
 Use IMG activity "Assign Currency Types to Accrual Item Types" to create entries for additional G/L currencies intended for display in review and approval screens. 
 Currency Type Requirements: 
 Only currency types that already exist in the General Ledger can be enabled. 
 To verify available currency types, access transaction FINSC_LEDGER and navigate to Company Code Settings for the Ledger. 

 Review and Approval:Thresholds for Periodic Accrual Amounts 
 Threshold Structure:  Two thresholds can be defined to control the review and approval process for periodic accrual amounts: 
 Upper Threshold : Accrual amounts exceeding this threshold require mandatory review and approval before posting. 
 Lower Threshold : Accrual amounts below this threshold will not be posted. 
 Automatic Approval Zone : Accrual amounts falling between the lower and upper thresholds are automatically approved without requiring manual review or approval. 
 Configuration Location:  Threshold variants are configured in the IMG activity "Define Accrual Item Types" under the "Item Type Settings for Ledgergroup and Representative Ledger" section, where a threshold variant can be entered. 
 Optional Usage:  The use of threshold variants is entirely optional. 
 Default Threshold Variant:  Threshold variants are defined separately in the IMG activity "Define Threshold Variants." When a threshold variant is marked as default, the system automatically applies this variant to Item Type Settings for Ledgergroup and Representative Ledger if no other variant has been explicitly entered. 

 Time Intervals for Performing Review and Approval 
 Restriction of Time Periods: 
 Review and/or approval time periods can be restricted in the system. 
 Time Interval Variants - Definition and Configuration: 
 Corresponding time interval variants can be defined and configured in two ways: 
 Enter them in the IMG activity "Define Accrual Item Types → Item Type Settings for Ledgergroup and Representative Ledger" 
 Mark the variant as default 
 Usage of time interval variants is optional. 
 Creation and Maintenance of Time Interval Variants: 
 Time interval variants for review/approval are created and maintained in the IMG activity "Define Time Interval Variants" 
 Time Intervals for Review and/or Approval Section: 
 Allows definition of start and end dates and times when review and approval are permitted 
 This is a current setting that can be performed in the productive system 
 Start and end dates and times are defined separately for each fiscal period 
 Since the Accrual Engine supports multiple frequencies beyond fiscal periods, identification occurs by using the Last day of the fiscal period

items.title: POAC Limitations
items.author: Balazs_Szauder
items.text:
Purchase Order Terms with Item Category "Limit" (Value B, EKPO-PSTYP = 1) 
 Delivery Schedule Issues: 
 Only one entry exists in the delivery schedule, making accrual calculations based on the schedule meaningless 
 Date Limitations: 
 No explicit start and end dates are available in the purchase order item for linearized distribution of the total amount 
 System defaults used instead: 
 Start date: Purchase order document date (EKKO-BEDAT) 
 End date: The single delivery schedule entry date 
 Amount Valuation Issue: 
 System uses purchase order item net value as the total accrual amount 
 The expected value field (ESUH-COMMITMENT) would be more suitable 
 Customization Option: 
 Use BAdI POAC_MMPO_2_ACE_TRANSFER or Enhancement Spot POAC_ACCR_OBJECT BAdIs for different accrual behavior 

 Purchase Order Terms with Item Category "Service" (Value D, EKPO-PSTYP = 9) 
 Delivery Schedule Issues: 
 Only one entry exists in the delivery schedule, making accrual calculations based on the schedule meaningless 
 Date Availability Constraints: 
 Start and end dates for linearization are only available: 
 When business function PSM_USFED_PEROP_1 is active (public sector) 
 In the Services tab of transaction ME23N (stored in tables ESLH and ESLL as ESLL-PER_SDATE and ESLL-PER_EDATE) 
 These tables are currently not evaluated by the system 
 Default Dates Used: 
 Start date: Purchase order document date (EKKO-BEDAT) 
 End date: The single delivery schedule entry date 
 Customization Option: 
 Use BAdI POAC_MMPO_2_ACE_TRANSFER or Enhancement Spot POAC_ACCR_OBJECT BAdIs for different accrual behavior

items.title: Datasphere OData API: support for joins and custom SQL
items.author: harsh324
items.text:
Hi Team, 
 We have a use case where a customer wants to run their existing custom logic through the Datasphere OData API. 
 Example (shown in SQL; we can translate it to another format for OData if required): 
 SELECT i.INSTALLATION, i.RATE_GROUP, MAX(b.BILL_END_DATE) AS LAST_BILL 
 FROM INSTALLATIONS i 
 JOIN BILLING_DOCS b ON b.INSTALLATION = i.INSTALLATION 
 WHERE i.RATE_GROUP IN ('IEE-BD','EDM-BD') 
 GROUP BY i.INSTALLATION, i.RATE_GROUP 
 HAVING DAYS_BETWEEN(MAX(b.BILL_END_DATE), CURRENT_DATE) > 30 

 We find that this query logic (in any syntax or format) cannot be used with the OData API. Here is what we found on the features Datasphere OData supports: 
 1. SAP Help for Datasphere OData lists only $select, $filter, $orderby, $top, $skip, $count, $batch and input parameters, on one asset per service URL. 
 2. S/4HANA OData services also support $expand (along modeled associations) and, for analytical services, $apply. So related-entity reads and aggregations can be pushed down in S/4HANA, but apparently not in Datasphere. 
 Not listed in the Datasphere OData docs: 
 3. Joins across multiple tables or views (inner and left) 
 4. Self-joins (a table joined to itself, e.g. comparing current and previous records) 
 5. Aggregation with GROUP BY / HAVING (MAX, COUNT, SUM; no $apply) 
 6. Nested and correlated subqueries (e.g. latest record per key) 
 7. CTEs (WITH clauses) 
 8. UNION / UNION ALL 
 9. Calculated columns (CASE, string functions like TRIM/REPLACE; no $compute) 
 10. Date functions in conditions (e.g. DAYS_BETWEEN against CURRENT_DATE) 
 We need help to confirm the following: 
 1. Are joins supported through the Datasphere OData API in any form? 
 2. Is the Datasphere OData API limited to the options above, so that #3–#10 are not supported (no custom SQL, $expand, $apply or $compute)? Is anything planned, and when? 
 3. For join-heavy logic like the example, what is SAP's recommended approach for an external tool to read the result from Datasphere: OData, SQL access, or something else? 
 Reference links: 
 - Datasphere, Consuming Data via the OData API: https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_DATASPHERE/43509d67b8b84e66a30851e832f66911/7a453609c8694b029493e7d87e0de60a.html

items.title: 5MQ combined with embedded TM (6W2/6W3/6W4) in S/4Cloud Public: restriction in note vs. working test
items.author: robin_barre1
items.text:
Hello everyone, 
 We are implementing SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (release 2608) and are assessing the activation of the embedded Transportation Management scope items 6W2 (Manual Transportation Planning), 6W3 (Transportation Execution) and 6W4 (Freight Settlement). 
 Context: 
 - Most of our outbound sales flows run on scope item 5MQ (Sell from Stock with Valuated Stock in Transit). Finance requires it: goods stay in valuated stock in transit after goods issue, and revenue and COGS are recognized at the transfer of control to the customer (incoterm based). 
 - The SAP document "Restrictions for the Transportation Management Processes" (2608.2, version 7.1.0) lists 5MQ among the "Not-Supported Processes". 
 - However, our consultants tested TM with 5MQ in our development system and the end-to-end flow worked as expected (freight unit, freight order, delivery, goods issue to VSIT, transfer of control). 
 - At the same time, Advanced Intercompany Sales (5D2), which also uses valuated stock in transit, is listed as supported with TM. 
 Our questions: 
 1. Has anyone implemented TM together with 5MQ in Public Cloud? Did you get any confirmation or exception from SAP, or run into issues in production? 
 2. What is the functional reason why 5MQ is not supported while 5D2 (also VSIT based) is? Is it a technical limitation or only a validation that SAP has not done yet? 
 3. If the combination stays unsupported, what alternatives would you recommend to keep the VSIT / transfer of control logic while using TM? 
 4. Is a removal of this restriction planned? Several restrictions in the same document were lifted in recent releases (5D2 and 5HP in 2602.2, 2TX and BMY in 2608.2). 
 Any feedback, experience or reference would be very helpful. 
 Thank you in advance!

items.title: Migrating REST Error Handling from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite
items.author: Qi_L
items.text:
When enterprises migrate from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite , the interface flow itself can usually be converted automatically by the Migration Tool . However, additional considerations may be required for the Error Handling rules configured in the REST Receiver Adapter .   
 In SAP Process Orchestration , error-handling behavior can be directly defined within the REST Adapter , such as Error Message, HTTP Status Code, HTTP Status Text. These configurations directly influence the error response returned to the caller at runtime. 
 Since SAP Integration Suite does not provide an equivalent adapter-level Error Handling mechanism, these configurations must be transformed into runtime logic within the Integration Flow during the migration process. 

 REST Error Handling in SAP Process Orchestration 
 The SAP Process Orchestration REST Receiver Adapter provides a flexible Error Handling configuration that allows interface developers to define how exceptions should be returned to the calling system. Instead of exposing the original runtime exception, custom conditions and response content can be configured directly within the adapter channel. 

 The error handling configuration supports several evaluation options, including: 
 Exception – Trigger error handling when an exception occurs. 
 HTTP Status Code – Evaluate the returned HTTP status code. 
 HTTP Status Text – Evaluate the returned HTTP status text. 
 HTTP Header Element – Check specific HTTP header values. 
 Text Content – Search for specific content within the response payload. 
 JSON Expression – Evaluate response content using JSON expressions. 
 XPath Expression – Evaluate XML response content using XPath expressions. 
 Always – Apply the configured action regardless of the response content. 
 These options enable both protocol-level checks (such as HTTP status codes and headers) and payload-level validations (such as XML or JSON content). As a result, a wide range of error-handling requirements can be implemented directly at the adapter level without additional process logic. 
 While these configurations are maintained as adapter settings in SAP Process Orchestration, SAP Integration Suite requires equivalent behavior to be implemented as executable integration flow logic, which introduces a migration challenge. 

 REST Error Handling in SAP Integration Suite 
 To achieve behavior equivalent to SAP Process Orchestration REST Adapter error handling, SAP Integration Suite provides several implementation options that can be applied within the integration flow. 
 A common implementation includes: 
 An Exception Subprocess to catch runtime exceptions 
 A Groovy Script to evaluate and process error information 
 A Content Modifier to construct the desired error response 
 Exchange properties or headers to store HTTP status codes and status texts 
 Migration Patterns for REST Adapter Error Handling 
 Although the SAP Process Orchestration REST Adapter provides several error handling sources, most migration scenarios can be consolidated into three generic implementation patterns in SAP Integration Suite. By focusing on these patterns rather than individual configurations, the migration process becomes more standardized and easier to automate. 

 Direct Response Handling 
 This pattern covers configurations where the response can be determined immediately without evaluating the backend response content. 
 Typical SAP Process Orchestration sources include: 
 Always 

 Exception 

 For the Always source type, the configured custom response is returned regardless of whether the receiver call succeeds or fails. To make this behavior work, the Throw Exception On Failure option in the receiver REST adapter must be disabled. If this flag remains enabled, the adapter throws an exception immediately when the receiver call fails, and the configured Always response is not returned to the caller. 
 During migration, this behavior is implemented directly in the main iFlow. After the receiver processing step, a Content Modifier constructs the predefined response payload and, if configured, the corresponding HTTP status information before the response is returned to the caller. 

 Unlike the Always scenario, where a predefined response is returned regardless of the processing outcome, the Exception scenario is triggered only when a runtime exception occurs. To preserve this behavior during migration, the Throw Exception On Failure option in the receiver adapter must remain enabled so that receiver-side errors are propagated as exceptions. 
 The migration generates an Exception Subprocess that intercepts processing errors and constructs the configured response message before it is returned to the caller. The Exception Subprocess must end with an End Event rather than an Error End Event . Otherwise, standard error handling is triggered and the default error response, including the MPL ID, is returned instead of the configured custom response. 
 Because the exception is handled within the Exception Subprocess and the integration flow completes normally, the corresponding MPL entry has the status Completed rather than Failed .   

 HTTP Metadata Validation 
 This pattern covers configurations that evaluate information contained in the HTTP response metadata. 
 Typical SAP Process Orchestration sources include: 
 HTTP Status Code 
 HTTP Status Text 
 HTTP Header Element 
 In the following example, the REST receiver channel uses HTTP Status Text as the error handling source. Whenever the returned status text contains the value NotFound , SAP Process Orchestration triggers a custom result and returns a predefined error message instead of the original response. 

 The generated flow follows the generic HTTP metadata validation pattern. The configured condition is evaluated against the HTTP response metadata available in the runtime exchange, for example: 
 ${header.CamelHttpResponseText} regex '.Not Found.' 
 A Router evaluates the configured condition. If the condition evaluates to true, a Content Modifier constructs the custom response defined in the original SAP Process Orchestration configuration, for example: 
 Custom Not Found 
 The flow then terminates with an Error End Event to preserve the error semantics of the original configuration. 
 If the condition evaluates to false, no custom response is generated and the integration flow reaches the normal End Event. 
 The generated flow follows the generic HTTP metadata validation pattern:   

 The same migration pattern is applied for HTTP Status Code and HTTP Header Element based error handling configurations. 

 Payload Validation 
 This pattern covers configurations that evaluate the content of the response payload itself. 
 Typical SAP PO sources include: 
 Text Content 
 XPath Expression 
 JSON Expression 
 These configurations allow error handling decisions to be based on business content rather than technical response information. 
 In the following SAP PO configuration, the REST receiver adapter uses Text Content as the error handling source. The adapter checks whether the response payload contains the text “ Timeout” . If the condition is met, the configured action is Ignore Error, meaning that the adapter does not raise a technical exception and message processing continues.   

 When migrating this scenario to SAP Integration Suite, the response body must first be analyzed because the condition cannot be evaluated directly from HTTP response metadata. 
 To support different SAP PO Text Content configurations, a generic evaluation pattern can be used. Firstly, the Throw Exception On Failure option in the receiver HTTP adapter must remain disabled. A Content Modifier stores the source type (for example, Text, XML, or JSON) and the configured matching expression as exchange properties.  

 A Groovy Script then reads these properties, evaluates the response payload accordingly, and stores the matching result as a boolean exchange property. 
 A subsequent Router evaluates this property isMatch and determines whether the configured error-handling action should be applied or whether processing should continue normally. If Response contains "Timeout", then ignore the error. 
 Generic Response Content Evaluation Script: import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message 
import groovy.json.JsonSlurper 
import groovy.util.XmlSlurper 

def Message processData(Message message) { 

 def props = message.getProperties() 
 String sourceType = props.get("SourceType") as String 
 String matchExpression = props.get("MatchExpression") as String 
 String payload = message.getBody(String) 
 boolean isMatch = false 

 if (payload && sourceType && matchExpression) { 
 switch (sourceType.toUpperCase()) { 
 case "TEXT": 
 String regex = 
 matchExpression 
 .replace(".", "\\.") 
 .replace("*", ".*") 
 isMatch = payload.matches("(?s).*${regex}.*") 
 break 

 case "JSON": 
 isMatch = payload.contains(matchExpression) 
 break 

 case "XML": 
 isMatch = payload.contains(matchExpression) 
 break 

 default: 
 isMatch = false 
 } 
 } 

 message.setProperty("isMatch", isMatch) 
 return message 

} 
 The script supports the migration of SAP PO payload-based error handling by evaluating the response payload against a configured matching expression and storing the result in the isMatch exchange property. This property can then be used by subsequent routing logic to determine whether the configured error-handling action should be applied. The same reusable approach can be extended to other payload-based error-handling sources, such as JSON Expression and XPath Expression , allowing migrated conditions to be evaluated consistently and the appropriate response behavior to be determined based on the evaluation result. 

 Conclusion 
 From a migration perspective, REST Adapter error-handling configurations can be grouped into three common implementation patterns based on the type of information used for evaluation: direct result handling, HTTP metadata validation, and payload content evaluation. 
 These patterns provide practical approaches for reproducing SAP Process Orchestration REST Adapter error-handling behavior in SAP Integration Suite. By mapping the original SAP Process Orchestration conditions to equivalent iflow components, organizations can achieve feature parity while preserving the intended runtime behavior of existing interfaces. 

 Additional references 
 FAQ – Migration from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite 
 Get Started with Migration to SAP Integration Suite (Discovery Center Mission) 
 Master Blog: SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration – Tool and Guidance

items.title: How to Use Joule Work in SAP Commerce Cloud Development
items.author: safin
items.text:
Overview 
 SAP Commerce Cloud development spans data modeling, Java extension development, OCC API customisation, ImpEx scripting, Backoffice configuration, Solr search tuning, integration design, and more. Joule Work, SAP's AI-powered desktop assistant, brings a conversational AI layer directly into that workflow, helping developers move faster, reduce context-switching, and tackle complex problems without leaving their working environment. 
 This post explores the practical ways SAP Commerce Cloud developers and architects can leverage Joule Work across the full development lifecycle — from researching documentation and generating boilerplate code to reviewing configurations, writing training content, and building reusable knowledge assets. 
 What is Joule Work? 
 Joule Work is a desktop AI assistant (available on macOS and Windows) that combines a large language model with access to your local file system, web search, terminal execution, Microsoft 365 integration, and an extensible connector and skill system. Unlike a browser-based chatbot, Joule Work works directly alongside your IDE, your project files, and your Commerce Cloud documentation, making it a genuine development companion rather than a separate lookup tool. 
 Key capabilities relevant to Commerce Cloud development 
 File access: read and write ImpEx, Spring XML, YAML, Java, and JSON files directly from your project folder. 
 Terminal execution: run Ant builds, scripts, and shell commands without leaving the conversation. 
 Web search: pull live documentation from help.sap.com and SAP Community on demand. 
 Skills: install domain-specific instruction sets (e.g. the SAP Commerce Cloud Expert skill). 
 Connectors : connect to external systems like Jira, GitHub, or MCP compliant Commerce Cloud environment. 
 Spaces: build persistent dashboards for architecture decisions, API references, and release tracking, etc. 
 Advanced Mode: switch to the deeper reasoning model for complex architectural or debugging questions. 
 Setting Up Joule Work for Commerce Cloud Development 
 The recommended setup steps are as follows: 
 Create the SAP Commerce Cloud Expert skill, this gives Joule documentation-backed answers based on help.sap.com. 

 Enable Web Search 
 Enable Advanced Mode, use it for architecture and complex debugging questions. 

 Set your project folder, this allows Joule to read and write project files. 

 Enable Extended Thinking, it's useful for understanding Joule's reasoning on complex problems 

 Create a project Space, use it to collect architecture decisions, API references, and release notes across development sessions. 

 Set Personal Instructions, so Joule always answers based on specific context. 

 Application Scenarios 
 Use Case 1: Documentation Research & API Reference Lookup 
 Commerce Cloud documentation is deep and spread across help.sap.com. Joule Work's web search capability lets you ask natural-language questions and get answers backed by verified SAP documentation links — without manually navigating the Help Portal. 
 Example prompts: 
 How does the Promotion Engine calculate cart-level discounts in SAP Commerce Cloud 2211? 
 What is the correct way to extend the OCC API without modifying commercewebservices? 
 Give me the ImpEx syntax to create a WebhookConfiguration linked to a POJO Integration Object? 
 Use Case 2: Code Generation 
 SAP Commerce Cloud development involves a lot of repetitive boilerplate — custom extension scaffolding, Spring bean declarations, ImpEx templates, FlexibleSearch queries, and Integration Object definitions. You can ask Joule Work to generate the code, review it in the conversation, then ask Joule Work to save it directly to the correct file path in your project. 
 Example prompts: 
 Generate an ImpEx to create a POJO Integration Object for SubmitOrderEvent with order code and timestamp fields. 
 Write a Spring bean definition for a custom CartValidationStrategy that checks minimum order quantity. 
 Generate a FlexibleSearch query to find all active products in the Electronics catalog with a price below 100 USD 
 Use Case 3: Architecture & Design Decisions 
 SAP Commerce Cloud projects regularly face design decisions — when to use Webhooks vs. Outbound Sync, how to structure a custom B2B approval workflow, when to extend OCC , how to model a custom promotion rule. Joule Work's Advanced mode excels at these multi-factor reasoning questions. 
 Example prompts: 
 Should I use a POJO Integration Object webhook or Outbound Sync to notify my OMS when an order is submitted? Compare both approaches. 
 We need to add a supplier management feature to SAP Commerce Cloud. What is the recommended extension architecture? 
 What are the trade-offs between extending Spartacus components vs. building a custom headless storefront? 
 Use Case 4: Debugging & Troubleshooting 
 When something goes wrong — a Solr indexing issue, an OCC API returning unexpected results, an ImpEx import failing — Joule Work can help you diagnose the problem by cross-referencing error messages with SAP documentation and your attached project files. 
 Example prompts: 
 I'm getting a `ModelSavingException` when saving a custom item type. What are the most likely causes? 
 This OCC response is returning a 401 even though I'm passing a valid OAuth token — what could cause this?" 
 Use Case 5: Spaces for Project Knowledge Management 
 Joule Work's Spaces lets you build persistent dashboards that collect cards from multiple conversations. For a Commerce Cloud project, this is useful for maintaining living reference documents across the team. During development conversations, ask something like "Add this architecture decision as a card to my Commerce Cloud Space". 
 Example Spaces to build: 
 Commerce API Reference: cards summarizing key OCC endpoints, Integration Object configurations, and webhook setups 
 Release Tracker: cards tracking 2211.x release notes, new features, and upgrade steps 
 Architecture Decisions: text cards capturing key design decisions with rationale and verified documentation links 
 Use Case 6: Skills for Repeatable Workflows 
 If your team follows a specific process for developing Commerce Cloud extensions — a standard review checklist, a code generation template, a release checklist — you can encode that process as a "Joule Work Skill" and share it across your team. 
 Example skills:: 
 Commerce Extension Reviewer: review a custom extension against SAP's best practice guidelines (no modifications to OOTB code, correct Spring structure, no cyclic dependencies) 
 ImpEx Validator: check ImpEx syntax and flag common mistakes before import 
 Summary 
 Joule Work integrates naturally into the SAP Commerce Cloud development workflow by bringing AI-assisted documentation lookup, code generation, architecture reasoning, and content creation directly to the developer's desktop without requiring a separate browser tab or tool switch. The combination of a domain-specific skill (SAP Commerce Cloud Expert), file access, terminal execution, and the Spaces feature makes it a practical day-to-day companion for developers, architects, and technical leaders working on Commerce Cloud projects. The key to getting the most out of it is giving Joule context: attach your files, set your project folder, describe your constraints, and use Advanced mode for the hard problems.

 SAP Commerce Cloud Development Best Practices

items.title: How Bestseller Turned Fragmented Workforce Data into Trusted People Intelligence
items.author: Andrea Domhardt
items.text:
Bestseller uses SAP SuccessFactors HCM and People Intelligence in SAP Business Data Cloud to replace fragmented, inconsistent workforce data with a single governed foundation, so leaders across all brands and countries work from the same numbers and focus on decisions. 

 When Kristoffer Buur joined Bestseller ’s people organization more than 10 years ago, the company was already a global fashion group with a broad portfolio of brands and stores. Today it counts more than 50 fashion brands and about 30,000 colleagues in around 45 countries. Its products are sold in about 2,800 branded chain stores and roughly 16,000 multi-brand and department stores across the world. Back then, it lacked a reliable answer to the most basic workforce question: how many people actually work here? 

 “We believed our headcount was around 12,000,” says Buur, who leads Global HR and People Technology Initiatives at the Danish fashion group. “When we brought everything together, the real number was closer to 20,000.” 

 No data had been falsified. No system had failed. The number was simply scattered across multiple systems, each counting differently. And that gap, nearly 8,000 people, is exactly what happens when a large, fast-growing organization runs on fragmented people data. 
 Drive better people and business decisions across hiring, retention, pay, and more with People Intelligence 

 Learn more 

 The real problem wasn’t the data. It was trust. 

 Bestseller’s challenge was not unique. HR teams at complex, multi-country organizations frequently find that the same metric—headcount, termination rate, open positions—produces a different answer depending on which system or team you ask. 

 The consequence is predictable. Meetings that should focus on what to do next become debates about which figure is correct. Leaders stop relying on the data. HR reverts to producing reports rather than enabling decisions. 

 Buur puts it plainly: “If two leaders look at the same question and reach two different answers, the meeting becomes a decision about the numbers, not about what to do.” 

 Before Bestseller could use data to act, it needed data it could trust. 

 Foundation first 

 “Everyone wants to talk about AI and prediction models. I understand why,” Buur says. “But it’s a bit like building a house. Most organizations want to start with the roof. We chose to start with the foundation.” That foundation is SAP SuccessFactors HCM, which Bestseller calls its “people system.” It now holds the full, clean employee lifecycle across every brand and country. 

 On top of it, Bestseller uses People Intelligence in SAP Business Data Cloud . This is where governance meets business context: definitions, rules, and retail-specific logic, such as store managers, weekly working hours, and location hierarchies, are encoded once and applied everywhere. 

 The result is a three-layer architecture that moves from raw data to decision support: 

 People system: SAP SuccessFactors HCM as the trusted source of workforce data 

 People Intelligence: the analytics layer, with governance definitions and Bestseller-specific business context 

 Decision layer: role-based views shaped for the leaders who use them, across countries, brands, and functions 

 What leaders see today 

 Every leader’s view brings the same perspectives together on one page: headcount, working hours, hires, terminations, and open positions. Each is compared to the previous month and the previous year, so leaders can see which direction they are moving in. Growth in stores and teams is visible across countries, brands, and functions, all from the same foundation. 

 In recruiting, Bestseller’s business is seasonal, and that rhythm is now visible before it arrives. “Our leaders could see those peaks coming and plan for them instead of explaining them afterwards,” Buur says. 

 Turnover is where the impact has been most significant. “We employ many young people, so of course we expect movement,” Buur says. “But there is a big difference between saying we have high turnover because we employ young people and actually seeing where and why.” 

 The early leavers view tracks terminations among employees with less than three, three to six, and six to nine months of tenure. Voluntary and involuntary terminations are shown alongside. A color-coded termination rate for every country means a leader can spot an issue in seconds. 

 The same numbers, everywhere 

 What makes the views meaningful is not what they show, but what sits underneath them. When a country’s HR team talks to headquarters about headcount or turnover, both sides are using the same definitions, the same rules, the same system. 

 Some markets have grown their headcount by a third or more in a single year, while their open positions have fallen sharply. Elsewhere, a single month’s hiring push, with many new hires and only a handful of leavers, is immediately visible. The early-leaver view then answers the follow-up question automatically: are those new hires staying? 

 Each type of leader sees a view shaped for their context. A retail leader sees store staffing, working hours, and hiring across the chain. A country leader sees growth, vacancies, and turnover in their market. A brand leader sees the workforce behind the brand across countries. The views differ, but the foundation and the governance are the same. 

 What changed 

 The shift Buur describes is concrete. Before People Intelligence, meetings started with “Which number is correct?” and HR produced reports for most of them. Turnover was explained after it had already happened. 

 Now the question is “What actions do we take?” Leaders spot patterns before they become problems. Data quality errors surface quickly, because leaders who trust the numbers do not want to be caught presenting incorrect ones, so they flag and fix them. 

 “Instead of debating which number is correct, our leaders focus on what to do,” Buur says. “That’s the change.” 

 Buur sums it up: “People Intelligence helped Bestseller make faster, more informed decisions by combining three things: trusted workforce data, governance, and role-specific leadership insights. If you put those together, you turn data into actionable business outcomes. For us, the journey goes from knowing what happened to understanding why, and step by step towards action before it happens.”

If you put those together, you turn data into actionable business outcomes. For us, the journey goes from knowing what happened to understanding why, and step by step towards action before it happens.” 

 Partnership matters 

 Bestseller was among the early customers working with People Intelligence. Buur credits two partners with making it work: SAP Consulting , who brought product expertise, and Effective People , who knew the SAP SuccessFactors landscape and Bestseller’s data. 

 “Instead of three parties speaking three different languages, we built one team that understands the business, the data, and the technology,” Buur says. “That’s what turned our wishes into something concrete.” 

 What comes next 

 People Intelligence at Bestseller is not a finished project. The company is building an absence report on the same foundation and plans to expand the coverage of report types. Each addition strengthens the data layer and moves the organization closer to acting before issues occur, rather than responding after them. 

 “This isn’t really about dashboards,” Buur says. “It’s about turning people’s data into insights, insights into actions, and actions into better decisions.” 

 The headcount question that once produced two very different answers, 12,000 or 20,000, now has one.

items.title: Dynamic Page Size for an Adobe Form (DDIC-based interface)
items.author: paibias
items.text:
We had a requirement to have the a SAP Document form to be printed in two paper sizes: A4 and Letter. Creating a form per paper-size makes maintenance difficult as both forms are generally the same, only varying in the paper size, but will require development to both forms for any changes required. 
 Now, this is something that is already taken care of in Output Management via the separation of master layout and content layout. So this solution is mainly for DDIC-based Adobe form outputs (NACE Adobe forms). 
 Some things to note: 
 Because the page size is dynamically picked, this can only work if the page sizes to be determined can accomodate the same content area size, particularly width-wise. Like for my case, I need to dynamically pick either A4 or LETTER. It can result to alignment issues or truncation if the content area varies greatly (ie. dynamically picking between A4 and A5) 
 This is made for scenarios where all the pages to be printed will have the same size, and with the last page set as "No Restriction" (ie. a NEXT PAGE that applies to all succeeding pages after PAGE1). The last master page without restriction serves as the boundary which prevents A4 printing to continue printing on to LETTER Page set. In my example, I have only 2 master pages per size: a FIRST PAGE and a NEXT PAGE (applies to all succeeding pages). This can work for more than 2 master pages, as long as they are in the order of how they will be printed and each master page other than NEXT is only printed with a max count (ie. Page1, Page2, Page2 and Next). So for scenarios where you have a subform that will be printed to a specific master page at a certain criteria, there might be additional steps necessary for that or possibly use of conditional pagination instead. 
 I'll just dive right to it 🙂 

 This is how my Hierarchy looks like: 

 Above we can see 2 page sets named (1) A4 and (2) Letter. Each has 2 Master pages named Page1 and Page2 . The first one being the first page, and the second being the "next" page, which is used for all other pages aside from the first one. 
 There is also a hidden subform where the paper size value is mapped to a text, for evaluation in scripts. This hidden subform can be skipped by accessing the data node directly in the scripts instead. 
 This is then followed by a Subform named for each master page set: A4 and LETTER. 
 Then followed by the normal contents subforms. In my case, there is only only one that is named BODY. 

 So, for the necessary settings. 
 This is how Page1 looks like. As you can see, this is only restricted to Max: 1. That means this master page will only be used once when printing the content. 

 Page2 has no restrictions, because this is whats going to be used for the rest of the pages: 

 The same can be observed in LETTER page set: 

 This next part can be skipped, as its possible to access the data directly in the script when evaluating. But for this case, I had mapped the value of PaperSize to a field wrapped in a Hidden Subform: 

 Now, for the PaperSize Subforms. 
 The idea is that these almost-invisible subforms will determine which Page1 to pick. Its that simple! 🙂 
 So you start by creating the subform. Let's start with LETTER. We create it as Flowed . If for some reason, you need this as Positioned , just create it as small as possible. This is to ensure the they will not affect the content subforms in any way: 

 Then under Pagination , set to place on Page1_Letter which is our master page for page 1 with Letter as size: 

 And then on the script, you just evaluate the PaperSize field value and hide it if not equal. Below is a sample code in JavaScript 

 The same steps is done for the A4 subform: 

 That's it! 🙂 
 As long as the content (BODY) subforms have pagination settings to Follow Previous and Continue Filling Parent, this basic setup will work. 

 It is also possible to do this via conditional pagination, but this is a simple, straight-forward method instead. Which I believe is perfect for ABAP developers who are new or learnign Adobe forms development. 
 Hope this helps! 🙂 

 Tips: 
 As I mentioned above, the content area on each master page should be able to accomodate the content subforms' dimensions. For our case, since Letter is wider than A4, we just designed the content area to be center-aligned in the page so as letter prints to not result with a wider right margin. 

 When troubleshooting, sometimes, its a bit difficult to see if it is the correct page size it is using, so during development/testing, I would mark each page of that size and which page name they are to help me determine what master page it is printing on.

 この計算方法ではケース1の結果は説明できますが、ケース2でSAPが 10 JPY と計算する理由を説明できません。 
 一方、SAPが最初に課税標準額を算出し、その後、税込金額と課税標準額との差額として税額を算出していると仮定すると、以下になります。

 164 ÷ 1.1 = 149.0909... → 149（Round Down） 
 164 - 149 = 15 JPY 
 ケース2 
 109 ÷ 1.1 = 99.0909... → 99（Round Down） 
 109 - 99 = 10 JPY 
 この計算方法ではケース2の結果は説明できますが、ケース1でSAPが 14 JPY と計算する理由を説明できません。 
 このような結果の違いがなぜ発生するのか、また、SAP内部で税コードV3の 課税標準額および税額がどのように計算されているのか について、ご教示いただけますでしょうか。 
 特に、 計算順序、内部的に保持される小数精度、および端数処理が適用されるタイミング について、情報をいただけますと幸いです。 
 最後までお読みいただきありがとうございます。

 5. 仮払消費税額および非控除税額は、端数処理後の課税基準額を基に算出されるのでしょうか。それとも、端数処理前の内部値を基に算出されるのでしょうか。 
 6. SSCUI 101016で確認済みの端数処理設定とは別に、計算精度または中間計算時の端数処理が、その他のパラメータ、条件タイプ、税計算表、通貨の小数桁設定、その他の設定によって制御されていますでしょうか。制御されている場合、該当する設定項目をご教示いただけますでしょうか。 
 例えば、税コードN2を使用して税込金額 JPY 1,010 を入力した場合： 
 （初期）課税基準額 = 1,010 / 1.10 = 918.181818...

key_points: Profiles let one codebase use SQLite in development and HANA in production.
The SQLite path must sit inside requires.db.credentials.url, otherwise CAP silently creates db.sqlite.

[production] kind hana; mbt build runs cds build --production

36.summary: The post explains how REST receiver error-handling rules from SAP Process Orchestration's REST adapter must be rebuilt as iFlow logic when migrating to SAP Integration Suite, since Integration Suite has no adapter-level equivalent. It lists the PO evaluation sources and groups most migrations into patterns. The Direct Response pattern (Always and Exception) and the HTTP Metadata Validation pattern are described in detail, with Throw Exception On Failure, Exception Subprocess end-event rules, and MPL status behaviour. The text is cut off in the middle of the HTTP Metadata Validation example, so the Router logic and any later patterns are not shown.
key_points: Integration Suite has no adapter-level error handling, so PO REST receiver rules become iFlow logic.
For 'Always', disable Throw Exception On Failure on the receiver adapter, or the configured response is never returned.
For 'Exception', keep Throw Exception On Failure enabled so receiver errors reach the Exception Subprocess.
The Exception Subprocess must end with an End Event, not an Error End Event, or the default error response with MPL ID is returned.
With a handled exception the MPL entry shows Completed rather than Failed.
HTTP Metadata Validation uses a regex on ${header.CamelHttpResponseText} routed by a Router.
technical_details: PO REST receiver error-handling sources: Exception, HTTP Status Code, HTTP Status Text, HTTP Header Element, Text Content, JSON Expression, XPath Expression, Always
Throw Exception On Failure (receiver REST adapter flag)
Integration Suite components: Exception Subprocess, Groovy script, Content Modifier, Router, exchange properties or headers
End Event versus Error End Event in the Exception Subprocess
Expression: ${header.CamelHttpResponseText} regex '.Not Found.'
MPL status Completed versus Failed
36.why_it_matters: Error responses returned to callers are an integration contract, so silently losing them during migration breaks clients. The flag and end-event rules are the non-obvious points that a converter will not preserve automatically.
36.developer_problem: How do I reproduce SAP PO REST adapter error-handling rules (custom response on Always, Exception, or status text) in an SAP Integration Suite iFlow after migration?
36.teaching_angle: Good migration exercise: give trainees a PO channel with HTTP Status Text set to NotFound, and ask them to build the iFlow equivalent with a Router and Exception Subprocess. Discuss the regex: the post's value is 'NotFound' but the expression tests 'Not Found' with a space, and the unescaped '.' matches any character, so trainees should check which one actually matches the HTTP reason phrase.

digest.headline: ABAP environment release 2611 adds CDS Define Index, RFC error details and more ADT tooling; the rest of the day is thin posts and unanswered questions.
digest.overview:
The main item is the SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment release 2611, delivered on November 14. It adds Define Index on CDS table entities, Get_Details and Get_Last_Error for RFC errors, authorization default variants (R3TR SUCO) in ADT for Eclipse, and more object types in ADT for VS Code. The post is a roundup and the detail sits on linked pages that we did not read.

The rest is mostly practical but shallow. The Adobe Forms dynamic page size post is the most concrete. The CAP posts cover profiles and a risky auth shortcut. The Integration Suite post covers REST error handling after migration from PO. Several Q&A threads (SHD0, Datasphere OData, Public Cloud iFlow triggers) are unanswered and work as teaching cases. Many posts are cut off or teasers, so treat their claims as unverified.

top_stories.title: ABAP environment release 2611: CDS indexes, RFC error details, SUCO in ADT
top_stories.summary: Release 2611 was delivered on November 14. CDS DDL `Define Index` creates unique, text and standard indexes on CDS table entities. RFC errors for communication-target calls can be read via `Get_Details` on exception objects and `Get_Last_Error` on session objects. Authorization default variants (R3TR SUCO) are maintainable in ADT for Eclipse. ADT for VS Code gains Service Consumption Model, Swagger for OData services and Transport Organizer. An ADT MCP Server is available for Eclipse and VS Code, and ABAP AI SDK can extract data from images into a RAP business object.

top_stories.title: Adobe Form with dynamic A4/Letter page size for DDIC-based NACE forms
top_stories.summary: One form uses two page sets (A4, LETTER), each with Page1 (Max 1) and a Page2 master with no restriction. A hidden PaperSize subform on each Page1 is hidden or shown by JavaScript. The BODY subform uses Follow Previous and Continue Filling Parent. Both page sizes need compatible content-area widths. The author notes Output Management's master/content layout split is preferred where available.

top_stories.title: REST error handling from SAP PO to Integration Suite must be rebuilt in the iFlow
top_stories.summary: Integration Suite has no adapter-level error handling. For 'Always', disable Throw Exception On Failure on the receiver. For 'Exception', keep it on and end the Exception Subprocess with an End Event, not an Error End Event. A handled exception shows Completed in the MPL. The HTTP Metadata Validation pattern uses a regex on `${header.CamelHttpResponseText}`, but the excerpt cuts off.

top_stories.title: CAP profiles: SQLite locally, HANA Cloud in production, and a dummy-auth shortcut to avoid
top_stories.summary: Profiles in `package.json` under `cds.requires.db` switch between SQLite and HANA. A misplaced path silently creates db.sqlite, and a wrongly named CSV seed file gives an empty table with no warning. Production `jwt` auth needs `@sap/xssec`. The author set auth to dummy, which the post itself calls trial-only. `cds env requires.db --profile production` shows the resolved config.

top_stories.summary: The documented options are $select, $filter, $orderby, $top, $skip, $count, $batch and input parameters, one asset per service URL. The asker needs joins, GROUP BY/HAVING and date functions, and notes S/4HANA Gateway offers $expand and $apply. No answer is given.

deep_dives.title: What release 2611 changes for ABAP developers: CDS indexes and RFC error details
deep_dives.explanation:
The source post is a roundup with one-line items, so what follows is limited to what it states. The CDS DDL statement `Define Index` now creates unique, text and standard indexes directly on CDS table entities. Previously secondary indexes were handled in a separate dictionary step. Verify the exact syntax on the linked detail page before using it in class.

For RFC calls using a communication target, error details are now available through `Get_Details` on the exception object and `Get_Last_Error` on the session object. The split suggests one path for exception-based handling and one for session-level state. The post does not explain the exact differences, so test both against a failing destination.

In ADT for Eclipse, authorization default variants (R3TR SUCO) can now be created and maintained. ADT for VS Code gains Service Consumption Model, Swagger for OData services, Transport Organizer, SQL Notebook, ATC exemptions and an ABAP Dictionary log. An ADT MCP Server is offered for both IDEs.

This is the ABAP environment release (BTP), not on-premise S/4HANA 2023. Do not tell trainees these features exist on their on-premise systems without checking.

deep_dives.title: Dynamic paper size in a DDIC-based Adobe Form
deep_dives.explanation:
The goal is one form printing on A4 or Letter without duplicates. Build two page sets, A4 and LETTER. Each has master pages Page1 (pagination Max = 1) and Page2 (no restriction). Page2 NEXT acts as the boundary between sets.

Place a small flowed subform `PaperSize` on the master Page1 of each set, bound to the paper-size value. A JavaScript script hides the one that does not match, so only the correct Page1 is used. Its pagination is set to Page1_A4 or Page1_Letter. The author mentions an optional hidden subform mapping the value to text for scripts, since the data node can be read directly.

The content subform BODY must use Follow Previous and Continue Filling Parent so pagination follows the selected Page1. The sizes must share compatible content-area widths, otherwise content is misaligned or truncated. The author centred the content area for Letter. With more than two master pages, order them in print sequence and set a max count on each non-NEXT page.

The author says Output Management's master/content layout split is preferred where available. The JavaScript and screenshots are not in the excerpt.

deep_dives.title: Migrating PO REST receiver error handling to iFlows
deep_dives.explanation:
PO's REST receiver adapter could evaluate several sources: Exception, HTTP Status Code, HTTP Status Text, HTTP Header Element, Text Content, JSON Expression, XPath Expression and Always. Integration Suite has no adapter-level equivalent, so each rule becomes iFlow logic.

For the Direct Response pattern with 'Always', disable Throw Exception On Failure on the receiver adapter. Otherwise the configured response is never returned. For 'Exception', keep it enabled so receiver errors reach the Exception Subprocess. The subprocess must end with an End Event. An Error End Event returns the default error response with MPL ID.

A handled exception shows Completed in the MPL instead of Failed, which affects monitoring. HTTP Metadata Validation uses a regex on `${header.CamelHttpResponseText}` routed through a Router.

Caution: the post's example tests 'Not Found' with a space while the PO value is 'NotFound', and an unescaped `.` matches any character. Check which string the real reason phrase matches. The text is cut off, so later patterns are unseen.
key_concepts: End Event vs Error End Event

*Don't fix a CAP production crash with dummy auth*

CAP in production uses `jwt` auth, which needs `@sap/xssec`.
Missing package = crash at startup.

One blog's workaround: set auth kind to `dummy`. The author says it's trial-only.

post_drafts.title: PO to Integration Suite errors
post_drafts.text:
*Migrating REST error handling from PO to Integration Suite?*

There's no adapter-level error handling in Integration Suite. Rebuild it in the iFlow.

- 'Always': turn *off* Throw Exception On Failure
- 'Exception': keep it *on*
- End the Exception Subprocess with a plain *End Event*, not Error End Event
- Handled errors show as Completed in MPL, not Failed

Check your regex too: 'NotFound' and 'Not Found' are different strings.

https://community.sap.com/t5/integration-blog-posts/migrating-rest-error-handling-from-sap-process-orchestration-to-sap/ba-p/14525134

interview_questions.question: Your CAP app works locally on SQLite but crashes on Cloud Foundry with 'Cannot find @sap/xssec'. How do you diagnose and fix it, and what is wrong with switching auth to dummy?
interview_questions.answer: In production CAP resolves auth to `jwt`, which requires `@sap/xssec` at runtime. A missing dependency crashes at startup, so first add the package to dependencies and bind an XSUAA service instance in the MTA. Use `cds env requires.auth --profile production` to confirm the resolved config. Setting auth kind to `dummy` removes authentication entirely, so anyone can call the service. That is acceptable only in a trial, not in a real project. Also check that the HANA profile is set for production and that the MTA build uses `cds build --production`.

interview_questions.question: You migrate a PO REST receiver channel with error handling 'Exception' to Integration Suite. What must be configured so the custom error response is returned, and how will monitoring look?
interview_questions.answer: Keep Throw Exception On Failure enabled on the receiver REST adapter, so receiver failures raise an exception that reaches the Exception Subprocess. Build the custom response there with a Content Modifier or Groovy script. End the subprocess with a normal End Event. An Error End Event returns the default error response with the MPL ID instead of your custom one. Because the exception is handled, the MPL status shows Completed, not Failed, so monitoring and alerting based on status must be adjusted. For the 'Always' rule you would instead disable Throw Exception On Failure, otherwise the configured response is never returned.

interview_questions.question: A client needs Datasphere data with joins and aggregates exposed to an external tool via OData. What is your design?
interview_questions.answer: The documented Datasphere OData API supports $select, $filter, $orderby, $top, $skip, $count, $batch and input parameters, one asset per service URL. It does not document joins, GROUP BY/HAVING, subqueries, CTEs, UNION or date functions. So the join and aggregation logic belongs in a Datasphere view (relational or analytical model), which is then exposed with simple filters. That also keeps logic centralised and pushed down to the database. For other access paths such as SQL access, check SAP's current documentation. I would also confirm whether limits are planned to change, since the thread has no roadmap statement. Compared with S/4HANA Gateway, which offers $expand and $apply, the design must move logic into the model.
